Cautiously hawkish. The FOMC raised the policy rate to 4.75–5% and continued quantitative tightening while emphasizing “cumulative tightening” and policy lags. It acknowledged that recent banking stresses will tighten credit and weigh on activity, hiring, and inflation, even as it underscored that “the U.S. banking system is sound and resilient.” Implementation moves—lifting the interest on reserve balances, calibrating ON RRP and standing repo, and maintaining balance sheet runoff caps—reinforce rate control and liquidity backstops.

FSR context tilts the assessment modestly more negative than a pure policy-read. The Financial Stability Report highlights persistent inflation and monetary tightening as top-cited risks, alongside market liquidity strains and volatility in core rates markets, and pressures on credit quality from higher rates (for example, leveraged loans). The SLOOS evidence of tighter lending standards, coupled with vulnerabilities in parts of the financial system, points to greater downside risks to growth even as bank capital/liquidity and standing facilities provide resilience.

Netting these, the communication is restrictive with elevated downside growth and credit risks, but not outright pessimistic. Relative to a neutral baseline, this warrants a slightly more negative sentiment than before.
